topIssues.title: ZKDisputeGame: a respected game can use an unrespected game as its parent
topIssues.author: Inphi
topIssues.body:
## Summary

A ZK game can start from its parent's claim. Its proof shows only that the transition from that claim is correct. `initialize()` checks that the parent did not lose, is not blacklisted or retired, has the same game type, and is above the anchor. It does not check the parent's `wasRespectedGameTypeWhenCreated`. `isGameClaimValid` checks only the child's flag.

So a claim that does not count, and that challengers may not watch, can become the start of a claim that counts.

## Where

- `packages/contracts-bedrock/src/dispute/zk/ZKDisputeGame.sol:346-368`: the parent checks.
- `packages/contracts-bedrock/src/dispute/AnchorStateRegistry.sol:331-353`: `isGameClaimValid`.

## Scenarios

1. **Rollout.** ZK is registered before it is respected. An attacker creates a ZK game with a forged root, and nobody challenges it. After ZK becomes respected, a respected child proves a correct transition from that forged root and becomes a valid claim.
2. **Incident.** A prestate bug forces a fallback to another game type. During the fallback, an attacker creates a ZK game that uses the bug. It is not retired, because it was created after the retirement time. After the switch back to ZK, a respected child of that game becomes a valid claim.

The FPVM games are not affected. They have no parents and always start from the anchor.

## Fix

Compute the child's respected flag first in `initialize()`. Then add:

```solidity
if (wasRespectedGameTypeWhenCreated && !parent.wasRespectedGameTypeWhenCreated()) revert InvalidParentGame();
```

Unrespected children can still use any parent, so proposal chains can continue after a switch away from ZK. Update the spec (`game-mechanics.md:124-126`) to match.

topIssues.title: op-node: static peer cannot be re-dialed after its peerstore address TTL expires ("no addresses")
topIssues.author: tuan-phan
topIssues.body:
**Bug Description**

`op-node` adds the addresses of each `--p2p.static` peer to the peerstore once, at startup, with a 7-day TTL (`op-node/p2p/host.go`, `initStaticPeers`). The reconnect loop (`monitorStaticPeers` -> `dialStaticPeer`) dials by peer ID only and never re-adds the configured addresses. Once the process has been up for more than 7 days, the first disconnect from a static peer is therefore permanent: every minute the node logs

```
lvl=warn msg="static peer disconnected, reconnecting" peer=<peer-id>
lvl=info msg="dialing static peer" peer=<peer-id> addrs=[/ip4/<ip>/tcp/9222]
lvl=warn msg="error reconnecting to static peer" peer=<peer-id> err="failed to dial <peer-id>: no addresses"
```

The `addrs` printed in the log come from the CLI config, but `DialPeer` only sees the peerstore, whose entry for the peer has expired, hence `no addresses`. If the static peer does not advertise a dialable address of its own through identify, nothing repopulates the peerstore. Restarting op-node makes the peer dialable again because `initStaticPeers` runs again.

On a chain whose recommended node configuration is a single `--p2p.static` sequencer peer plus `--p2p.no-discovery`, this leaves the node with zero gossip peers: it stops receiving unsafe payloads, the unsafe head falls back to what L1 derivation yields (minutes behind the sequencer tip) and `optimism_syncStatus` reports `unsafe_l2 == safe_l2`. We hit this on several nodes at once after the sequencer peer closed its connections, about a week after the nodes had started; nodes restarted the day before reconnected without any issue.

#12113 reports the same symptom (same log lines, "restarting the validator node allows it to reconnect again"); the 7-day TTL explains why it only shows up on nodes with long uptimes.

**Steps to Reproduce**

1. Start op-node with `--p2p.static=/ip4/<ip>/tcp/<port>/p2p/<peer-id>`. Adding `--p2p.no-discovery` makes the impact visible (no other peers), but is not needed for the dial failure itself.
2. Keep it running for more than 7 days, so the static peer addresses expire from the peerstore.
3. Have the static peer close the connection (restart it, or disconnect from its side).
4. Watch the op-node log: the reconnect attempt fails every minute with `failed to dial <peer-id>: no addresses`, and `opp2p_peers` reports `totalConnected: 0` when there are no other peers.

The same failure can be reproduced in a unit test without waiting 7 days, by clearing the static peer's addresses from the peerstore after a disconnect and calling `dialStaticPeer` again; on `develop` it fails with exactly `failed to dial <peer-id>: no addresses`. A PR with that test and a fix follows.

**Expected behavior**

The configured addresses of a static peer are available for every reconnect attempt, so a static peer can be re-dialed for as long as the process runs, regardless of uptime.

**Environment Information:**

- Operating System: Linux (containers on Kubernetes), amd64
- Package Version: op-node v1.19.7 and v1.19.8; the relevant code in `op-node/p2p/host.go` is unchanged on `develop` (dfe4f947)

**Configurations:**

```
--p2p.static=/ip4/<ip>/tcp/9222/p2p/<peer-id>
--p2p.no-discovery
--p2p.listen.tcp=9222
--p2p.advertise.ip=<public-ip>
--p2p.peerstore.path=/data/op-node/peer
--p2p.discovery.path=/data/op-node/discovery
```

**Logs:**

See the block above; it repeats once per minute until op-node is restarted. On the same node, `optimism_syncStatus` shows `unsafe_l2` equal to `safe_l2` and several minutes old, and `opp2p_peers` shows `totalConnected: 0`.

**Additional context**

Workaround without a restart: `opp2p_connectPeer` with the full multiaddr of the static peer, since `host.Connect` re-adds the addresses before dialing. The proper fix is to re-add the configured addresses in `dialStaticPeer` before `DialPeer`.

topIssues.title: kona-node: NetworkActor stalls the p2p swarm for the duration of a remote-signer HTTP call
topIssues.author: geoknee
topIssues.body:
## Summary

`NetworkActor::step()` awaits the block signature **inline in its `select!` arm**. With a remote signer that is an HTTP round-trip, and until it resolves `step()` has not returned — so the `select!` is not re-entered and no other arm is serviced, including the libp2p swarm event stream.

This is the kona-node counterpart of #22554, but the victim is different. In op-node a slow signer was subtracted from the next block's build window. Here the sequencer is already insulated (see below); what stalls instead is **p2p processing**.

There is also **no deadline** on the signing call, so a signer connection that hangs rather than errors wedges the network actor indefinitely.

## The code

`crates/node/service/src/actors/network/actor.rs`, one `select!` (line 107) whose `publish_rx` arm (line 136) signs before publishing:

```rust
Some(block) = self.publish_rx.recv(), if !self.publish_rx.is_closed() => {
    // ...
    let signature = signer.sign_block(payload_hash, chain_id, sender_address).await?;   // :151 blocks here
    match self.handler.gossip.publish(selector, block, signature) {                     // :153
```

While that future is in flight, none of the sibling arms run:

| Arm | What stops |
| --- | --- |
| `self.handler.gossip.next()` (:159) | the libp2p swarm event stream — inbound block gossip is not consumed |
| `unsafe_block_rx` | inbound unsafe blocks are not forwarded to the engine |
| `handler.enr_receiver` | discovered peers are not dialed |
| `peer_score_inspector.tick()` | peer scoring / monitoring |
| `admin_query_rx`, `p2p_rpc_rx` | admin `PostUnsafePayload`, p2p RPC |

`RemoteSigner`'s HTTP client is built without a timeout — `build_http_client` (`crates/node/sources/src/signer/remote/client.rs:103`) calls `reqwest::Client::builder()` and never sets `.timeout(...)`, and there is no timeout anywhere under `crates/node/sources/src/signer/`. reqwest's default is no request timeout.

## What is *not* affected

The sequencer does **not** block on the signer, which is worth stating because it is the part op-node got wrong:

- `SequencerActor::seal_and_commit_payload_if_applicable` hands the payload off via `schedule_execution_payload_gossip` (`actors/sequencer/actor.rs:207`).
- That trait is documented as fire-and-forget: "should return as quickly as possible and offers no guarantees that the payload actually was gossiped successfully" (`actors/network/gossip.rs`).

Two caveats on that insulation:

1. It is still a bounded `mpsc::Sender::send().await`, so it is not immune — just deeply buffered. The channel is capacity **256** (`service/node.rs:469`), i.e. ~8.5 minutes of 2s blocks before the sequencer feels backpressure.
2. 256 in-flight payload envelopes is a large memory ceiling, and the implied overflow policy is "eventually block the sequencer". For comparison, the op-node fix (#22585) deliberately chose a much smaller bound that drops the oldest entry rather than ever making the sequencer wait, on the grounds that an ungossiped block still reaches other nodes via L1 and derivation or other sync mechanisms, whereas a sequencer that stops building produces nothing for anyone. The two implementations currently disagree on that trade.

## Suggested fix

1. **Get the `await` out of the `select!` arm.** Sign and publish from a dedicated task rather than inside `step()`, so the swarm keeps being polled during the round-trip.
2. **Keep publishing ordered and bounded.** A single signing task draining a bounded queue preserves seal order — a verifier cannot follow the chain past a block it never received over gossip alone — and bounds memory well below 256 envelopes.
3. **Put a deadline on the signing call**, on the reqwest client or via `tokio::time::timeout`. This is what turns a hung signer from degraded gossip into an indefinitely wedged network actor, and it stands on its own.
4. **Choose the overflow policy deliberately**, and ideally make it agree with op-node's.

## Confidence and how to confirm

This is a **structural finding from reading the code; it has not been measured.** Whether a few hundred milliseconds of unpolled swarm meaningfully degrades inbound gossip in practice is unverified — gossipsub has internal buffering and may absorb it. The unbounded-wait case (hung signer, no timeout) is the unambiguous one.

To confirm the degraded-but-not-hung case, run a kona-node sequencer against a remote signer with injected latency and watch whether inbound unsafe-payload handling and peer scoring stall in step with the signing round-trips.

## Related

- #22554 — the op-node instance of the same shape (sequencer build window rather than p2p)
- #22585 — the op-node fix, including the ordering/bounding/overflow discussion

topIssues.title: l1-watcher: a transient L1 RPC failure on one chain kills the whole node
topIssues.author: claude
topIssues.body:
In the kona-node L1 watcher, one chain's failure is fatal to the whole node. When a chain's `eth_getLogs` request for system config logs fails — a transient L1 RPC error is enough — or a chain's derivation channel is closed, `L1WatcherActor::step` (`rust/kona/crates/node/service/src/actors/l1_watcher/actor.rs`) returns `Err`. The actor runner at `rust/kona/crates/node/service/src/service/util.rs:33` treats any actor error as fatal: it cancels every actor, and the host exits.

This predates the multi-chain watcher change in #22567 — a single-chain kona-node dies the same way when its L1 RPC hiccups, and transient L1 failures should never kill the node. At N > 1 chains served by one watcher the blast radius grows: one chain's transient L1 error stops every other chain in the host.

From the review discussion on #22567 (https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/pull/22567#discussion_r3838547816):

> Indeed this seems like a bug in even the current kona-node because transient L1 failures should never kill the node. We should log an issue for this and then create a follow up PR to fix it properly.

A follow-up PR will add per-chain fault handling: transient RPC errors retried or skipped rather than propagated as fatal, and per-chain isolation so one chain's failure does not stop the others.

Part of #22531.

topIssues.title: contracts-bedrock: fix StandardValidator for migrated interop members
topIssues.author: 0xOneTony
topIssues.body:
Interop migration retains each member’s `ProxyAdmin`, while the shared dispute contracts and `ETHLockbox` use the first member’s admin. `StandardValidator` assumes these shared contracts use the admin of the chain being validated.

For non-first members, shared proxy implementation lookups therefore revert, even with `allowFailure` enabled. Migration-specific validation succeeds, but ordinary validation fails immediately after migration and after subsequent upgrades.

**Definition of done**

- Resolve the shared admin from the `DisputeGameFactory` when validating an interop member.
- Verify the shared admin’s expected PAO owner and require shared contracts to use the same admin.
- Preserve per-chain admin checks and validation of non-interop chains.
- Test ordinary validation of both members after migration and upgrades, including the override path used by upgrade tasks.

topPRs.title: contracts-bedrock: Per-chain Review Period
topPRs.author: 0xarktos
topPRs.body:
Closes [#686](https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism-private/issues/686)

## Description

Makes the withdrawal review period configurable per chain. `PROOF_MATURITY_DELAY_SECONDS` (OptimismPortal2) and `DISPUTE_GAME_FINALITY_DELAY_SECONDS` (AnchorStateRegistry) move from constructor immutables on the shared implementations to per-chain proxy storage, set at `initialize()` and changeable through an L1PAO-only setter. The implementations keep a min/max pair of constructor immutables that bound every write.

OPCM carries each chain's live value forward on upgrade. The Migrator preserves each portal's and legacy registry's value and gives the shared AnchorStateRegistry the value the legacy registries agree on. op-deployer takes the delays as per-chain inputs and the bounds as implementation inputs.

Of the ~2,000 lines added, 786 are Solidity tests, 183 are regenerated snapshots, and most of the 576 Go lines are gofmt realignment of struct literals that gained the longer bound field names. The reviewable contract change is ~460 lines.

## Design decisions

- Storage, not immutables: `proofMaturityDelaySeconds` lands in portal slot 64 and `disputeGameFinalityDelaySeconds` in registry slot 7, both tagged `@custom:network-specific`. The existing getters keep their selectors, so every reader of the delays is unaffected.

- `initialize()` and the setter share one internal `_set…` that bounds-checks, stores and emits the `…Set` event, following `SystemConfig._setGasLimit`.

- Bounds are constructor immutables with getters, standard `[1 d, 7 d]` for proof maturity and `[12 h, 3.5 d]` for the finality delay. The constructor and `DeployImplementations` reject `min == 0` and `min > max`; there is no chain-id floor in the deploy script, since VerifyOPCM checks the bound immutables at release and the StandardValidator pins the implementation.

- No `upgrade` override for the delays due to the contract size limit on the OPCM. `_loadFullConfig` reads the live getters and passes them back to `initialize()`; `overrides.cfg.proofMaturityDelaySeconds` / `…disputeGameFinalityDelaySeconds` are not allow-listed and are rejected as unknown instructions. The setters are the only write path after deployment; For atomic upgrade and delay setting batch the calls in the same superchain-ops batch.

- Due to the contract size limit, OPCM does not validate the delays and the values are checked directly on the implementation.

- It is assumed that on the time of interop migration, chains will share the same delays. The shared ASR is initialized with the finality delay every chain's registry reports, or `migrate()` reverts with `OPContractsManagerMigrator_DisputeGameFinalityDelayMismatch` before any portal is touched. The shared-registry `initialize` moved into `_initializeSharedAnchorStateRegistry` because evaluating the agreement check inline in `migrate()` hits stack-too-deep.

- `StandardValidator` gains range checks (`PORTAL-100`, `…-ANCHORP-80`): "standard" now means within the sanctioned range. `VerifyOPCM` verifies the bound immutables on the implementations (`EXPECTED_MIN_/MAX_…` env vars with standard defaults) instead of a delay value the implementation no longer holds.

- op-deployer: the delays move from `SuperchainProofParams` to `ChainProofParams` under the same JSON keys, so existing `globalDeployOverrides` keep working and per-chain `deployOverrides` can differ; the bounds take their place as implementation inputs. `op-devstack` and `op-e2e` widen the bounds for their short devnet delays.

- Versions: OptimismPortal2 6.0.0, AnchorStateRegistry 5.0.0 (constructor and `initialize` ABI change, reinit versions bumped), OPContractsManagerStandardValidator 4.1.0, OPCM V2 9.0.3 (lands in the in-development 9.x release).

## Tests

Contracts, from `packages/contracts-bedrock`:

- `just pr` — build, lint, snapshots, semver-lock, interfaces, spacers, semgrep, size check.
- `just test-dev --match-contract 'OptimismPortal2_|AnchorStateRegistry_|OPContractsManagerV2_Deploy_Test|OPContractsManagerStandardValidator_|DeployImplementations_|DeployOPChain_|VerifyOPCM_|Initializable_|SetDisputeGameImpl'` — setter and `initialize` matrix (access control, bounds, events), delay changes applied to already-proven withdrawals and already-resolved games, deploy stores the delays in proxy storage, bounds errors on deploy, rejected override keys, StandardValidator range codes, VerifyOPCM bound checks.
- `DEV_FEATURE__OPTIMISM_PORTAL_INTEROP=true just test-dev --match-contract OPContractsManagerV2_Migrate_Test` — portal and legacy-registry delays preserved, shared registry inherits the agreed value, mismatch reverts.
- `just test-dev --match-path test/invariants/OptimismPortal2.t.sol` — the ProxyAdmin owner is excluded as a sender so the fuzzer cannot move the window under the invariants.
- `just test-upgrade` (needs `ETH_RPC_URL`) — `test_upgrade_withdrawalDelaysUnchangedWithoutOverride_succeeds` proves the 7 d / 3.5 d carry-forward through the real upgrade path.

Go, from the repo root:

- `just lint-go` passes.
- `go test ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/opcm/... ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/pipeline/... ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/state/... ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/bootstrap/ ./op-chain-ops/interopgen/...` — struct mirrors load against the current script ABIs on both the script-host and forge paths, `ResolveChainProofParams` defaults and per-chain overrides, bootstrap `Check()` bound cases.
- `go test ./op-deployer/pkg/deployer/integration_test/ -run TestProofParamOverrides` — bounds verified as implementation immutables, delays verified in portal slot 64 and registry slot 7 of the deployed proxies.

## Additional context

`op-deployer bootstrap implementations` replaces `--proof-maturity-delay-seconds` and `--dispute-game-finality-delay-seconds` with `--min-/--max-proof-maturity-delay-seconds` and `--min-/--max-dispute-game-finality-delay-seconds` (env `…_MIN_/MAX_…`). Operators who set the delays through `globalDeployOverrides` are unaffected; the keys now configure the chain rather than the implementation. Chains whose live delay is outside the bounds cannot upgrade until they redeploy; every production chain is at 7 d / 3.5 d.

- [Design doc](https://app.notion.com/p/oplabs/Per-chain-airgap-and-DelayedWETH-delay-proposed-changes-and-design-3e5f153ee162809ca7ebc1cf92d1e2ab)

topPRs.title: op-node: publish gossiped blocks off the sequencer's hot path
topPRs.author: geoknee
topPRs.body:
Fixes #22554.

`SimpleAsyncGossiper` published inline in its select loop, so while a publish was in flight the loop could receive nothing. With a remote signer that publish is an HTTPS round-trip, and the sequencer reaches `Clear()` 1–2 ms after `Gossip()` — so it blocked for the rest of the round-trip, and since the next build window is computed as a residual, that stall came 1:1 out of the next block's building time.

Publishing now runs on a dedicated goroutine; `Gossip`, `Get` and `Clear` only take a mutex, so none of them waits for the network.

### Design points the issue asked to pin down

- **Store-on-success is kept**, but guarded by an epoch counter that both `Gossip` and `Clear` advance. A publish that completes after a `Clear` cannot repopulate the reuse buffer — this preserves the invariant the blocking `Clear()` used to give for free (buffer empty before the next `Get()`), so the sequencer can never reuse a payload it has already inserted and moved past.
- **`Clear` does not cancel an in-flight publish.** Peers need the block either way; `Clear` only drops the payload held for reuse.
- **Overlapping publishes**: payloads are handed over through a single pending slot, and one publish runs at a time. A payload that has not started publishing yet is superseded by a newer one (logged) — the tip is what peers need, and they reach the older block through sync.
- **`Get` no longer waits** for an in-flight publish, so it can return `nil` where it previously blocked and then returned the payload. In that case the sequencer seals (or re-seals) its building job instead, which is strictly cheaper than stalling the build window.

### Hardening

A publish attempt now carries a deadline (`publishTimeout`, 10s — generous against any block time, so it never cuts a working signer short). Without it, a signer connection that hangs rather than errors blocked publishing until TCP gave up, and before this change block production with it. op-node's only remote block-signing path runs through this call, so the deadline covers it; instrumenting `op-service/signer`'s RPC client with the metrics recorder (the attribution gap noted in the issue) is left as a follow-up.

### Testing

`TestAsyncGossiperDoesNotBlockOnPublish` and `TestAsyncGossiperOverlappingPublishes` fail on the parent commit with exactly the reported symptom (`Get/Clear blocked until the in-flight publish returned`, `Gossip blocked until the in-flight publish returned`) and pass here. `TestAsyncGossiperConcurrentHandoff` hammers the handoff to confirm the non-blocking wake signal never loses a payload. `./op-node/...` is green, and `async`/`sequencing`/`driver` are green under `-race`.

### Review

Reviewed against `docs/ai/go-dev.md` directly rather than by dispatching `go-code-reviewer` — this session was configured without subagent dispatch. `./linter/bin/op-golangci-lint run ./op-node/...` reports 0 issues and `go mod tidy -diff` is clean.

topPRs.title: kona-node: recover from RPC failures without cascading across chains
topPRs.author: teddyknox
topPRs.body:
A transient L1 RPC failure in the watcher currently escapes as an actor error and shuts down the host, including unrelated chains. Simply logging and skipping the failed block is insufficient: if that block contains a signer rotation, the node can retain the wrong signer indefinitely. A closed derivation channel has the same excessive failure scope.

The broader problem is that recovery needs the semantics of the operation, not just the RPC. Configuration needs to converge to current state; engine work must survive outages without losing ordering; gossip becomes stale. A universal infinite-retry policy cannot distinguish these cases and can leave a shared actor stuck on one dependency.

The three commits address those levels. The watcher reads signer state from `SystemConfig` at the canonical head and retries failed reads, so missed rotations and reorgs converge without replaying every log. Engine operations retain pending work and retry with backoff; signing runs outside the network event loop with bounded attempts, allowing later payloads to proceed after an outage. Individual RPC deadlines bound stalls without cutting off healthy, long ancestry traversals. Independent per-chain watcher workers isolate slow RPCs, full queues, and closed channels; head updates can coalesce because consumers need the latest state. Losing every chain still terminates the watcher.

Added regression scenarios cover:

- Missed signer updates, recovery without a new head, same-height reorgs, and stale results arriving during an RPC or while the signer queue is full.
- L1/L2 reset failures, completion of the original reset request with a full derivation queue, long healthy resets, individual RPC timeouts, FIFO recovery of queued engine work, and signer failure followed by successful signing of a later payload.
- Healthy-chain head/finality/query progress while another chain stalls, chain-local channel closure, and cancellation of outstanding RPCs on shutdown.

304 affected-crate and downstream RPC tests pass locally. All CI checks and five required merge gates pass. Rust, recovery, reconciliation, and state-lifecycle reviews are complete; existing public error variants are retained for API compatibility.

Closes https://github.com/ethereum-optimism/optimism/issues/22655

topPRs.title: kona-node!: bound engine RPCs at the transport and add a SignerActor
topPRs.author: joshklop
topPRs.body:
Stacked on #23125 as a proposed simplification of its engine RPC deadlines. Draft while we iterate.

#23125 bounds engine RPCs in three separate places:
- `rpc_timeout` around individual call sites
- a timeout inside `record_call_time`
- an outer timeout around the reset forkchoice update

A new call site without the wrapper has no deadline. This PR removes all three and puts one deadline on each of the engine client's two RPC clients, the JWT Engine API client and its L1 client. Both get the same alloy transport layer, a stock tower `MapFutureLayer` that wraps each request in a timeout. The call sites are back to their form on `develop`.

Every request from the engine client now has a deadline, including ones #23125 does not wrap:
- `eth_getProof` for `optimism_outputAtBlock`
- payload bodies and client version
- capability exchange, so a stalled Engine API endpoint now fails the startup JWT check instead of hanging it

The deadline is on alloy's transport future, not on the hyper client below it. hyper's future completes when the response headers arrive, and alloy reads the body after that. A timeout at the hyper level would let an endpoint that stalls mid-body hang the call. The new test covers both a request that is never answered and a response whose body stalls after its headers.

Behavior otherwise matches #23125:
- The deadline is still per request, so a long reset traversal is not cut off.
- A timeout is still a transport error, so the engine classifies it as temporary and retries it as before.
- `new_payload_v1` keeps the `record_call_time` wrapper that #23125 added, which now only records its latency metric like the other Engine API methods.

The L1 watcher's timeouts are unchanged. They use the node's shared L1 provider, which derivation also uses, and a deadline there needs a separate decision.

It also proposes restructuring how the sequencer's blocks are signed:

- **The L1 watcher is the source of the unsafe block signer.** Each L1 watcher chain owns a watch channel for the signer, seeded with the value read at startup. Gossip validation and block signing subscribe to it. In #23125 the L1 watcher sends each signer to the network actor over a bounded channel, and the network actor relays it into the gossip crate's own watch channel. Publishing to a watch channel cannot block, so the refresh loop no longer reserves channel capacity before sending.
- **Signing moves into a `SignerActor`** between the sequencer and the network actor. #23125 signs in a task inside the network actor that gives each payload three 2s attempts and then skips it, so a transient signer outage leaves a gap in gossip. The `SignerActor` signs payloads in order and retries transient failures (remote signer transport errors and per-attempt timeouts) with backoff until they succeed, so nothing is skipped. Other signing errors are fatal, as before. If the signer rotates between signing and publishing, the payload is still published and peers reject it. The network actor goes back to only publishing.

Effect on operators:
- A remote signer outage longer than the sequencer's 256-payload queue pauses block production until the signer recovers, and the sequencer keeps answering admin RPC throughout, so op-conductor can still stop it. The backlog is then gossiped in order. With #23125 the sequencer keeps producing blocks and skips gossip for blocks it failed to sign. A long outage is meant to page someone.
- The block signer, including a remote signer's startup health check, starts only in sequencer mode. A validator with a signer configured logs that it is ignored.
- A kona-node in sequencer mode now fails at startup without a block signer (`--p2p.sequencer.key`, `--p2p.sequencer.key.path`, or `--p2p.signer.endpoint` with `--p2p.signer.address`). Before, it started and dropped every payload, so its blocks were never gossiped. op-node still allows this, but there it is only useful with p2p disabled, which kona does not support. The kona-node sequencer docs and CLI reference now list the signer flags.

BREAKING CHANGE: a kona-node started with `--mode sequencer` and no block signer now fails to start; configure one of the signer flags above. The rest affects code built on the `kona-gossip` and `kona-node-service` crates.
- `GossipDriverBuilder::build` returns only the driver, `GossipDriverBuilder::with_unsafe_block_signer_receiver` takes a `watch::Receiver<Address>`, and `GossipDriverBuilder::new` and `GossipDriver::builder` are no longer `const`.
- `NetworkBuilder::new` loses its `signer` parameter, and `NetworkBuilder::with_signer` is removed. `NetworkDriver` and `NetworkHandler` lose `signer` and `unsafe_block_signer_sender`.
- `NetworkActor::new` loses its signer-update receiver and takes a receiver of `SignedPayload` instead of unsigned payloads. `L1WatcherChain::new` takes a `watch::Sender<Address>`.
- `NetworkDriverError::BlockSignerStartError` and `NetworkActorError::{FailedToSignPayload, SigningTask, MissingUnsafeBlockSigner}` are removed.
- `SignerActor::new` takes a `BlockSignerHandler`; the actor always has a signer.
- `UnsafePayloadGossipClient` has a new required method, `has_capacity`, which the sequencer checks before sealing.

To migrate: give the L1 watcher chain the sender of a signer watch channel and pass its receiver to `NetworkBuilder::with_unsafe_block_signer`. To gossip a sequencer's blocks, start the `BlockSigner` and run a `SignerActor` between the sequencer's payload channel and the network actor's publish channel. Callers with a fixed signer keep passing an `Address` to `NetworkBuilder::new`.

Reviews: `rust-code-reviewer` was run on each commit. For the transport commit, its main finding, that a hyper-level timeout misses a stalled response body, is fixed. `deletion-reviewer` was run on the signer commits. It found no surviving references to the removed APIs outside code, and its findings are applied: the breaking changes are marked, a dead error variant is removed, and the kona-node design doc lists the signer actor.

topPRs.title: kona-sp1: reject untrusted chain configs in production guests
topPRs.author: Inphi
topPRs.body:
Production SP1 proofs must use the chain rules embedded in the guest. Accepting configs from unverified preimages lets a prover change the deposit contract and derive fake deposits. Range and consolidation reject chains whose complete configs are missing from the embedded registry.

Native execution receives trusted deployment configs directly. The executor, proposer, and canary retain their config-file overrides for witness collection; the SP1 guest independently enforces its embedded registry. Full-ELF tests use the opt-in `test-config-fallback` feature so synthetic chains can share one test ELF without rebuilding for each deployment. Production prestate builds reject an enabled test feature, a test-marked build SHA, or the dedicated unsafe-config marker embedded in the ELF. Custom registry inputs currently support only Mainnet, Sepolia, and Holesky as L1s.

Ordinary CircleCI and scheduled smoke tests share the same test-feature ELF build. The local and CI guest lint recipe also checks the feature-free production path, without another ELF build. Cargo and local build defaults remain feature-free. Prestate reproducibility rebuilds released tags rather than the PR head.

The acceptance runner extracts the L1 chain config from its genesis file before passing it to the executor. Passing the whole genesis previously made custom L1 chain IDs default to 1 and fail native witness collection. A focused regression checks the actual executor argument file preserves the chain ID and fork activation times. Config validation, resolver coverage, and synthetic-chain build instructions also address the review feedback.

Local validation passed: 41 host and core Rust tests, six guest tests, guest lint in both feature modes, scoped Rust Clippy, the acceptance argument regression, full custom Go lint and module checks, and CI wiring checks. The acceptance regression and empty-consolidation diagnostic failed before their fixes and passed afterward. Real native ELF builds earlier confirmed the unsafe marker is present with the test feature and absent without it. Full devnet acceptance was not run locally. CI is running for the current head.

Fixes #23207.
